claims.text: The starting alloy has composition Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 and an FCC matrix.
The as-manufactured alloy has a high dislocation density.
Additive manufacturing produces a refined grain-boundary network in this alloy.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by a balance between elemental synergy and processing-induced microstructural features.
Al and Cr act synergistically to form protective multilayer oxides in the target alloy.
Dislocations and grain boundaries mediate elemental diffusion and oxide-scale continuity.
A strongly oxidizing atmosphere promotes formation of a continuous protective scale on this alloy.
Under oxidizing conditions, Al and Cr rapidly produce a multilayer scale containing Al2O3 and Cr oxides.
The continuous oxide scale protects the substrate and slows degradation.
In reducing atmospheres, a high density of dislocations and grain boundaries accelerates oxygen ingress.
Accelerated oxygen ingress in reducing atmospheres disrupts oxide-scale continuity and increases degradation.
A controlled thermal treatment can lower dislocation density while preserving the overall FCC phase.
Lowering dislocation density diminishes fast diffusion pathways.
Lowering dislocation density yields a more coherent oxide scale under less oxidizing conditions.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a well-adhered, continuous multilayer scale and slower degradation than reducing exposure.
Reducing exposure will produce a less continuous, more defective scale and a higher degradation rate.
Thermally treated samples will have better scale integrity and lower degradation than the as-manufactured baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 1200 °C across atmospheres ranging from pure oxygen to H2/CO-rich reducing gas.
Oxide thickness, morphology, composition, weight change, and mechanical-property degradation can distinguish the proposed mechanism.
The hypothesis is falsified if neither atmosphere nor dislocation-density modification causes statistically significant differences in scale characteristics or degradation rates.
